#### A call for redesigning American streets

![September 6, 2018: A call for redesigning American streets](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1f66c44134aeaf736a7005e3c5)

**Duration:** 00:21:09

**Released:** 2018

**Series:** Better Off

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/5tv31geSxNlyz9aGq1ivib)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/2TDswhCVfRb4CNBlGEMVfM)

In this week’s podcast we’ll explore how America’s streets can be redesigned to benefit bicyclists and pedestrians—and we’ll explain why doing so may even help mitigate the effects of climate change. A new study from Anne Lusk, research scientist in the Department of Nutrition at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, analyzed how bicyclists and pedestrians responded to various placements of trees along cycle tracks—barrier-protected bicycle-exclusive paths between the road and the sidewalk. The research shows that the placement of these trees can play an important role in how people walking and biking perceive traffic, pollution, heat, and even safety. But the benefits extend beyond just those using the street—and could even be a factor in mitigating the effects of climate change. These trees may make it more likely that people will bike—helping to reduce pollution. And increased greenery can also help cool cities, which often suffer from a heat island effect, which means they’re significantly warmer than more rural areas. Lusk says all of this highlights the need to re-think how we’re designing streets to encourage more people to walk and bike instead of drive.

:::

A new study from Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health found that students who lived in dormitories without air conditioning during a heat wave performed worse on a series of simple tests compared with students who lived in air-conditioned dorms. The findings show that the effects of extreme heat are not just felt by those typically thought of as vulnerable—such as the elderly. And with global temperatures on the rise, the research underscores the need for sustainable design solutions in mitigating the health impacts of extreme heat. In this week's episode, we'll speak with the authors of that study to learn how we can  better design our buildings and cities to adapt to our changing climate. You'll hear from Joe Allen, assistant professor of exposure assessment science and director of the Healthy Buildings Program at the Center for Climate, Health, and the Global Environment, and Jose Guillermo (Memo) Cedeño Laurent, associate director of the Healthy Buildings Program.

#### How America Traded Its Walkable Cities for Parking Lots

##### How America Traded Its Walkable Cities for Parking Lots | Boring History for Sleep

![How America Traded Its Walkable Cities for Parking Lots | Boring History for Sleep](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1f695508bdc7eb9fb7c455e7f8)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/3K57vHeztR0HKUbKeXtEnx)

American cities were once built around people on foot. Downtown streets were packed with shops, apartments, streetcars, theaters, restaurants, and neighborhoods where daily necessities could often be reached without getting into a car. Then, after World War II, America began rebuilding its cities around the automobile.This video explores how highways, suburban expansion, urban renewal, zoning, and massive parking requirements transformed the American landscape. The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956 accelerated construction of the Interstate Highway System with the federal government covering 90% of Interstate construction costs. Meanwhile, suburbanization surged: in 1950, 23.3% of Americans lived in suburbs, but by 2000 that figure had reached 50%.Entire urban neighborhoods were demolished or divided by freeways and redevelopment projects, while historic buildings and downtown blocks were increasingly replaced by roads, garages, and surface parking. Parking minimums later reinforced car-oriented development by requiring businesses and housing projects to dedicate substantial amounts of land to automobiles.Discover how America went from compact, walkable neighborhoods to sprawling suburbs and parking lots—and why many cities are now trying to reverse the transformation.ResourcesInterstate System – Federal Highway Administration – FHWA Interstate System History1950 Census Records: A Window to History – U.S. Census Bureau – U.S. Census BureauAmerican Place: The Historic American Buildings Survey at Seventy-Five Years – National Park Service – National Park ServiceUrban Renewal and the Post-War American City – U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development – HUD ArchivesParking Spaces/Community Places – U.S. Environmental Protection Agency – U.S. EPA

#### How Congestion Pricing Can Impact Human Health

![How Congestion Pricing Can Impact Human Health](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1fb592b5cfd7631d9aa38b898d)

**Duration:** 00:17:50

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/5UpA5Uw23B6bukC0TABffC)

In early June, New York Governor Kathy Hochul blocked a congestion pricing plan from going into effect in New York City. This plan would have charged a fee for cars to enter the central business district of Manhattan, and it would have been the first congestion pricing plan to be fully implemented in the United States.While congestion pricing can be costly for commuters, the fact that it keeps some cars off the road means it can have health benefits for surrounding communities. Successfully implemented congestion pricing plans in cities such as London, Singapore, and Stockholm have led to better air quality and health.SciFri’s John Dankosky sits down with Dr. Janet Currie, co-director of Princeton’s Center for Health and Wellbeing, and Dr. Andrea Titus, assistant professor of the Department of Population Health at the NYU Grossman School of Medicine, to talk about the health impacts that congestion pricing has had around the world as well as the potential effects it could have in New York City and in other cities in the United States.Transcripts for each segment will be available after the show airs on sciencefriday.com. #### How to build an equitable and just climate future

##### TED Climate: How to build an equitable and just climate future | Peggy Shepard

![TED Climate: How to build an equitable and just climate future | Peggy Shepard](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1f1a24a475eee8709f1ec2b8fb)

**Duration:** 00:13:40

**Released:** 2024

**Series:** Speed & Scale

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/7J7oIbZW7bZ0BEILHsNjJA)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/72ezi2ePUkfWQGkoe85oWk)

Everyone has the right to a clean environment — but major disparities exist when it comes to who faces the consequences of pollution. Environmental justice leader Peggy Shepard points to the disproportionate impact that hazardous environmental conditions have on Black, brown and Indigenous communities and challenges us to build a truly equitable future that turns "sacrifice zones" — where community health is sacrificed for the sake of development — into "green zones" that redress the legacy of pollution and harmful policies.For the full text transcript, visit ted.com/podcasts/speed-and-scale-transcript Hosted on Acast. See acast.com/privacy for more information.

LED light bulbs are the future. They're better for the environment and the pocket book. But for some people, certain LEDs lights — particularly holiday lights—are also a problem. They flicker in a way that causes headaches, nausea and other discomfort. #### Right-Sizing Traffic Enforcement for Safer Roadways

About this episode:   The U.S. stands out among peer countries for having the worst rate of traffic deaths. Approaching this issue from a public health angle can help to make roadways safer by focusing on population-level interventions rather than directing resources towards policing "bad apple" individuals. In this episode: Tiffany Joyce Smith, lead author of a new report on the role of enforcement in road safety, explains the value of a proactive approach to preventing crashes versus a reactive one. Guest:   Tiffany Joyce Smith, MPH, is a public health and mobility expert and program advisor with the Vision Zero Network. Host:  Dr. Josh Sharfstein is distinguished professor of the practice in Health Policy and Management, a pediatrician, and former secretary of Maryland's Health Department. He served as the Baltimore City Commissioner of Health from 2005 to 2009.  Show links and related content:    Right-Sizing the Role of Traffic Enforcement: Prioritizing Effective, Cost-Efficient and Equitable Improvements to Road Safety—Vision Zero Network   Money Drove Criminal Justice System In Ferguson, DOJ Report Says—NPR   The Surprising Benefits of Narrower Traffic Lanes—Public Health On Call (November 2023)   Why Are So Many Pedestrians Getting Struck and Killed By Cars, and Why Aren't We Doing More To Stop It?—Public Health On Call (July 2023)   Transcript information: Looking for episode transcripts? #### What can design do for public health?

![March 22, 2019: What can design do for public health?](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1f5ca9d415bf1c9327cc50295b)

**Duration:** 00:45:36

**Released:** 2019

**Series:** Better Off

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/0dtXS3fRHN7ybA3KR0TMVN)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/2TDswhCVfRb4CNBlGEMVfM)

When many people think of design they’re probably picturing a product, like a new smartphone or car. But the design principles that lead to the creation of those products—such as the focus on human behavior or the use of prototyping—can also be harnessed to tackle complex public health challenges. In this week’s episode you’ll learn how one of the world’s top public health researchers, Ashish Jha, dean for global strategy at Harvard T.H Chan School of Public Health and director of the Harvard Global Health Institute, and one of the world’s foremost design experts, Patrick Whitney, professor in residence in the Department of Health Policy and Management, have teamed up to think about how design methods can be used to address issues ranging from the opioid epidemic to the future of hospitals. Full Transcript: hsph.me/design-pod This episode is a collaboration with Harvard Global Health Institute.

#### Why are scientists planting tiny forests in big cities?

![Why are scientists planting tiny forests in big cities?](https://i.scdn.co/image/ab67656300005f1f644d6e6a158e6aa90066442e)

**Duration:** 00:12:12

**Released:** 2026

**Series:** Short Wave

::: {.callout-description collapse="true"}

[Open Episode in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/episode/3cfiEXiP8KRa48ACkl2pMQ)

[Open Series in Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/2rTT1klKUoQNuaW2Ah19Pa)

Healthy forests help combat climate change, provide humans with drinking water and even improve mental and physical health. But it’s hard to imagine an entire forest in the middle of a big city. That’s where micro-forests come into play — public forests on a smaller scale, filled with native plants. They exist around the world, and producer Rachel Carlson went to visit the largest micro-forest in California in this encore episode. She joins host Emily Kwong to chat about what she saw. Interested in more of the science behind urban nature? ##### Description

Accessory Dwelling Units, or ADUs, are small, fully-functional secondary homes located on the same property as a main home (usually in the backyard) that serve as carriage houses or "granny flats." But as wildfires have displaced residents in the West, ADUs have filled a vital need where housing has proved scant or expensive. Correspondent Lee Cowan looks at the practical and legal challenges to making ADUs available. [Original air date: May 17, 2026.]

##### Video (1:06)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/XLnllIkjSFc title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Smoking in multi-unit housing poses serious health threats to children and adults even if no one smokes in their home. In multi-unit housing like apartment buildings and condominiums, secondhand smoke from one unit can move into other units. Smoking in multi-unit housing can also lead to fires, which can have deadly consequences. The videos below feature stories from residents, firemen, and public health advocates who have worked to make multi-unit housing properties smokefree.

#### A public housing project where healthy living is the foundation

**PBS NewsHour**, *07 07, 2017*

##### Video (6:29)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/iXT_KYahGzQ title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

In downtown Denver, a recently built public housing project is designed to foster healthy living, with access to nutritious food, access to doctors and ease of exercise and public transportation. Jeffrey Brown reports.

##### Transcript

**0:00** · JUDY WOODRUFF: But first: an experiment in rethinking public housing that encourages healthier living by changing the larger environment for residents.

**0:09** · Jeffrey Brown reports from Denver.

**0:12** · JEFFREY BROWN: At age 71, Noel Taylor says she's become more active and health-conscious than ever before.

**0:19** · NOEL TAYLOR, Denver: Every year, I improve my diet, I improve my exercise.

**0:25** · JEFFREY BROWN: Her change in behavior didn't happen by accident.

**0:28** · Four years ago, here in downtown Denver, Taylor joined an experiment in making healthy living part of the design and daily life of a public housing project.

**0:38** · Among the amenities here, access to a garden plot.

**0:42** · NOEL TAYLOR: I noticed, all summer long, I was getting healthier.

**0:45** · The more of my own vegetables I was eating, the more energy I had.

**0:51** · It's made a huge difference.

**0:52** · JEFFREY BROWN: So, this sounds all too good to be true.

**0:54** · NOEL TAYLOR: I know.

**0:56** · (LAUGHTER) JEFFREY BROWN: And there's more.

**0:58** · The Denver Botanic Gardens hosts a farmers market giving away free produce to residents.

**1:03** · WOMAN: We're going to talk about how to shop healthy on a budget.

**1:06** · JEFFREY BROWN: Another group offers classes on healthy recipes and shopping.

**1:10** · MAN: Now we will take your blood pressure.

**1:12** · JEFFREY BROWN: In a clinic on the ground floor of one building, public health physicians schedule regular visits to do routine checkups.

**1:19** · There's a light rail stop, both for easy transportation and to get residents out of their cars.

**1:25** · MAN: Do the other side now.

**1:27** · JEFFREY BROWN: Plus, bike rentals and a nearby shop to teach kids how to maintain their bikes.

**1:33** · Even the architecture and public art was designed to encourage residents to get outside and take a walk.

**1:40** · ISMAEL GUERRERO, Director, Denver Housing Authority: We really wanted this to look like a neighborhood, not a development.

**1:43** · JEFFREY BROWN: Ismael Guerrero, director of the Denver Housing Authority, says that, 10 years ago, this was a high-crime neighborhood, with 250 units of rundown public housing.

**1:55** · Something had to be done.

**1:56** · ISMAEL GUERRERO: What we learned in early conversations with residents in particular was, they didn't just want a new unit to move into.

**2:04** · They wanted a better quality of life.

**2:05** · So we really started expanding our perspective on what we were trying to accomplish here.

**2:10** · JEFFREY BROWN: The result completed earlier this summer is the Mariposa development, a mixture of 800 apartments and town homes, one-third public housing, a third subsidized, and a third rented at market value.

**2:24** · The overall cost was $150 million; $60 million came from federal, state and local government programs, with the rest coming through private investment.

**2:34** · Already, Mariposa is becoming a model for rethinking public housing.

**2:39** · ISMAEL GUERRERO: Part of it is physical health, and part of it is what we call neighborhood health.

**2:45** · Right?

**2:46** · How healthy is the place?

**2:47** · Is it safe?

**2:48** · Are there healthy activities for you to do?

**2:50** · Is there healthy food in the neighborhood for you to go and eat?

**2:53** · Is there a healthy economy where people can get jobs and start a business?

**2:56** · JEFFREY BROWN: The Osage Cafe, located in one of the apartment buildings, is designed to meet some of those needs.

**3:04** · In addition to the food, it provides culinary training and internships for young people in the neighborhood, like 20-year-old Israel Trejo.

**3:12** · ISRAEL TREJO, Denver: And I think that's where I discovered I had a passion for cooking.

**3:15** · JEFFREY BROWN: What did it give you?

**3:16** · ISRAEL TREJO: It gave me the entire world, basically.

**3:19** · Like, with the skills that I have learned now, I could go anywhere.

**3:23** · I could go be anything.

**3:24** · JEFFREY BROWN: Trejo now has a job at one of Denver's top restaurants, and plans to operate his own food truck soon.

**3:30** · ANGELA RODRIGUEZ, Denver: Are you looking forward to helping me grow some fruits and vegetables?

**3:36** · JEFFREY BROWN: Angela Rodriguez, a single mother of two teens, dreams of one day buying her own home.

**3:42** · She has a full-time job at a nearby community college, but Denver's booming housing market makes ownership difficult.

**3:50** · She lives in a subsidized town home at Mariposa, which she says is very different from the old-style projects she grew up in nearby.

**3:57** · ANGELA RODRIGUEZ: As a new style of public housing, it did take me a little bit of time for the adjustment.

**4:03** · When new tenants are mingling with other tenants that come from different walks of life, it's helping us to develop into new perspectives of modern living.

**4:13** · JEFFREY BROWN: Rodriguez uses public transportation, has taken up gardening, and has fully embraced the culture of health that is promoted here.

**4:22** · But is Mariposa working?

**4:24** · It's too early for definitive answers.

**4:27** · According to a 2015 study by the Denver Public Health Department, about half the residents had participated in health-related activities over the previous three years.

**4:38** · But the study also showed the amount of exercise residents pursued had changed little.

**4:43** · Just over a third said they exercised five times a week.

**4:47** · About the same amount said they exercised one to four times a week, and 26 percent said they rarely or never exercised.

**4:55** · Smoking rates decreased, but only slightly, from 30 percent of residents down to 24 percent.

**5:01** · And these so-called active staircases, designed with a bit of whimsy...

**5:05** · ISMAEL GUERRERO: It's a way to engage kids, and actually now the adults enjoy it.

**5:09** · JEFFREY BROWN: ... to lure residents away from using the elevator.

**5:12** · Well, so far, they're not having a big impact.

**5:15** · THERESA MICKIEWICZ, Denver Public Health: We actually did observational counts, where we sat there and we counted people who used the stairs vs. people who used the elevator, and we compared it against a control staircase in the Mariposa redevelopment, and we found absolutely no difference.

**5:32** · JEFFREY BROWN: Theresa Mickiewicz, an epidemiologist with Denver Public Health, is overseeing a study of the development.

**5:38** · And while major improvements in health remain to be seen, she believes something important is happening here, and she expects the numbers to reflect that soon.

**5:47** · THERESA MICKIEWICZ: While maintaining my objectivity as an evaluator, do I think that there is value in this type of project?

**5:55** · I would say yes.

**5:57** · Individually, these components have been shown in the evidence, in literature, to improve health outcomes.

**6:04** · JEFFREY BROWN: The city of Denver is so confident in this new model, it's about to embark on a similar development that will be three times larger than Mariposa.

**6:13** · That construction is expected to begin later next year.

**6:17** · For the "PBS NewsHour," I'm Jeffrey Brown, reporting from Denver.

**0:13** · Gene: That, of course, is Chris Rock’s famous joke about streets named for Martin Luther King Jr., which tend to be in -- let's say distressed areas.

**0:22** · And he’s not wrong, because if you look at the way housing segregation works in America you can see how things ended up this way.

**0:28** · Once you see it, you won't be able to unsee it.

**0:31** · OK, let’s look at MLK Boulevard in Baltimore.

**0:35** · I want to show you how to see housing segregation in schools, in health, in family wealth, in policing.

**0:41** · But first, an explanatory comma.

**0:45** · It’s the 1930s in the wake of the Great Depression.

**0:47** · FDR is president.

**0:48** · He wants to bring economic relief to millions of Americans through a collection of federal programs and projects called The New Deal.

**0:54** · One part of that "new deal" was The National Housing Act of 1934, which introduced ideas like the 30-year mortgage and low, fixed interest rates.

**1:03** · So now you have all these lower-income people who can afford homes, but how do you make sure they don't default on their new mortgages?

**1:09** · Enter the Home Owners Loan Corp.

**1:12** · The HOLC created residential security maps.

###### RESIDENTIAL SECURITY MAPS

**1:15** · And these maps? They're where the term redlining comes from.

**1:20** · Green meant “best area, best people,” aka businessmen; blue meant “good people,” like white-collar families; yellow meant a “declining area,” with working class families; and red meant “detrimental influences, hazardous," like “foreign-born” people, “low-class whites," and -- most significantly -- “Negroes.”

**1:41** · Again and again on these HOLC maps, one of the most consistent criteria for redlined neighborhoods is the presence of black and

brown people.

**1:49** · Let’s be clear.

**1:50** · Studies show that people who lived in redlined areas were not necessarily more likely to default on their mortgages.

**1:57** · But redlining made it difficult — if not impossible — to buy or refinance.

**2:02** · So landlords abandon their properties.

**2:04** · City services become unreliable.

**2:06** · In most places, crime increases.

**2:09** · And property values drop.

**2:11** · All of these conditions fester for 30 years as white people flee to the brand new suburbs popping up all over the country.

**2:18** · Many of those suburbs institute rules, called covenants, that explicitly forbid selling homes to black people.

**2:23** · And all of this was perfectly legal.

**2:27** · Now it’s 1968.

**2:29** · And MLK is assassinated.

**2:31** · News Report: Good evening.

**2:32** · The Rev. Dr. Martin Luther King, 39 years old, The apostle of nonviolence in the civil rights movement has been shot to death in Memphis, Tenn.

**2:39** · Martin Luther King was shot and was killed tonight in Memphis, Tenn.

**2:42** · In the aftermath, Congress passes the Fair Housing Act of 1968.

**2:47** · It's a policy meant to encourage equal housing opportunities regardless of race, or religion or national origin.

**2:52** · And it offers protections for future homeowners and renters, but does little to fix the damage already done.

**2:58** · Over the next 50 years, the Fair Housing Act is rarely enforced.

**3:02** · So you can still see housing segregation and its effects, in Baltimore and often along any MLK Boulevard in any U.S. city.

**3:11** · Like its effects on wealth.

###### WEALTH

**3:13** · So homeownership is the major way Americans create wealth, right?

**3:16** · Well, discrimination in housing is the major reason that black families up and down the income scale have a tiny fraction of the family wealth that white families do -- even white families with less education and lower incomes.

**3:28** · For almost 30 years, 98 percent of FHA loans were handed out to white borrowers.

**3:33** · Not only were black neighborhoods redlined, and not only was the Fair Housing Act selectively enforced, if at all, but it is still today much harder for a black person to get a mortgage or home loan than it is for a white person.

**3:46** · John: Families are fearful of speaking up about a basic human right that should be afforded to everyone in the world but definitely in the richest country in the world.

**3:59** · And housing segregation in schools.

**4:02** · The primary way that Americans pay for public schools is by paying property taxes.

**4:07** · People who live in more valuable homes have better-funded local schools, better-paid teachers, better school facilities and more resources.

**4:15** · Here’s a feedback loop: The better the schools in a neighborhood, the more those homes in that neighborhood are worth.

**4:21** · And the higher the property values of those homes, the more money there is for schools.

**4:25** · And so on and so on.

**4:27** · And housing segregation in health.

**4:29** · Because of urban planning that benefited those richer, whiter neighborhoods, people of color are more likely to live near industrial plants that spew toxic fumes; they're more likely to live far away from grocery stores with fresh food, and in places where

the water isn’t drinkable.

###### HEALTH

**4:43** · They're more likely to live in neighborhoods with crumbling infrastructure, and in homes with toxic paint.

**4:49** · Karen: When you're living with rats, roaches, and things like that -- that's deplorable.

**4:53** · You cannot have that kind of stuff with children running around in the building.

**4:56** · A building that may be full of lead.

**5:00** · And, not coincidentally, people of color have higher incidences of certain cancers, asthma and heart disease.

**5:08** · And housing segregation in policing.

###### POLICING

**5:11** · Housing segregation means we are having vastly different experiences with crime and vastly different experiences with policing.

**5:17** · Because our neighborhoods are so segregated, sometimes racial profiling can be camouflaged as spatial profiling — where living in certain areas can make you more likely to be stopped by the police.

**5:29** · And it means people have a lot of unnecessary contact with the criminal justice system just because of where they live.

**5:38** · Reggie: The problem in our city?

**5:41** · The police and the citizens are fighting.

**5:43** · They keep targeting my brothers and sisters who don't really have nothing.

**5:49** · And that heavy, aggressive kind of policing that you see in black neighborhoods in particular makes people feel like they can’t trust the police.

**5:55** · And when people don’t trust the police, crimes go unsolved and people have to find other ways to keep themselves safe.

**6:03** · But, of course, it’s not just Baltimore.

**6:05** · Because housing segregation and discrimination fundamentally shape the lives of people in nearly every major American city.

**6:14** · It really is in everything.

**6:18** · To hear more about how race shapes American life, visit npr.org/codeswitch.

**6:23** · I'm Gene Demby. Be easy.

##### Description

We took a field trip to the largest green roof in New York City. Then we imagined what the city could be like if all of its roof space was green.

##### Transcript

###### Intro

**0:01** · This is the largest green roof in New York City.

**0:04** · It's in the middle of bustling Manhattan, on top of the Javits Convention Center— a behemoth of a building with a six-block footprint.

**0:13** · But the roof hasn't always been green.

**0:16** · Before 2014, it was totally barren.

**0:20** · Now, just a few years later, when people walk out onto the roof, they say things like: "Amazing," "That's great," "I didn't expect this," "What a surprise."

**0:28** · But besides the great reactions, there are practical benefits.

**0:31** · We have 300,000 bees.

**0:34** · We've seen 25 different species of birds on the roof.

**0:36** · We reduced the temperature up here by about six degrees Fahrenheit.

**0:39** · And we also save about 7 million gallons of stormwater runoff that's absorbed in the soil and the plants that are on our roof.

**0:46** · We've been able to reduce our energy

consumption by about 26 percent, and that translated for us last year

into a saving of about 3 million dollars.

**0:55** · That is impressive.

###### Green Roofs

**0:58** · How does one green roof get so much done?

**1:01** · And what are all of the NOT green roofs in New York City doing with their lives?

**1:06** · First, let's see how much roof space actually exists.

**1:09** · You know, they are a major part of urban landscapes.

**1:12** · The the round number that most of us think exists is about 1 billion square feet.

**1:18** · One billion with a 'b.'

**1:20** · That's like 22 times the size of Central Park, in roofs.

**1:24** · And in most cities, what isn't roof is another impermeable surface like road, sidewalk, or parking

lot.

**1:31** · And these surfaces create a lot of problems for cities That green roofs can actually help solve.

###### stormwater runoff

**1:38** · Let's take a look at three of these issues. The first is

stormwater runoff.

**1:42** · Rainwater goes in pipes. It combines

with what's called sanitary water.

**1:48** · When there's too much rainwater, which happens hundreds of times a year around Manhattan, the wastewater treatment

systems shut down, and valves just let the water just,  you know, shunt out into the rivers. You know, it's got human sewage.

**2:01** · It's the biggest source of pathogens to

the Manhattan Island.

**2:04** · With green roofs, that water instead of going into the

drain and polluting the environment, ends up just evaporating the atmosphere

through the leaves of these plants.

###### heat island effect

**2:13** · And then, there's what scientists call the "heat island effect," which basically means that cities are significantly warmer than the surrounding areas.

**2:20** · I've seen asphalt roofs get up easily 170, 180 degrees Fahrenheit in the strong sunlight.

**2:26** · They absorb about 90 to 95 percent of the sunlight.

**2:30** · Green roofs, by comparison are close to air temperatures.

###### habitat loss

**2:34** · Another problem green roofs can help solve is habitat loss.

**2:37** · Cities can shrink or destroy the green space that's crucial for certain plants and

animals to survive.

**2:43** · Currently a lot of species might occur in  smaller parks throughout the city that are relatively unconnected, But having high densities of green roofs would allow those patches to be more connected.

**2:53** · Letting, for example, butterflies travel from patch to patch with lots of stepping stones of green roofs in between.

**2:59** · And these are just three of the problems that green roofs can help solve.

###### conclusion

**3:03** · But to really put a dent in any of these issues cities would have to implement green roofs at a large scale.

**3:09** · Stuart Gaffin, the research scientist

you heard from earlier, estimates that if all of New York City's 1 billion square feet of roof space were greened, those green roofs could lower the city's

temperature by nearly two degrees Fahrenheit and absorb over 10 billion

gallons of stormwater each year.

**3:27** · As cities continue to grow, all that empty roof space starts to look more and more like an opportunity, an untapped resource, a future ecosystem of problem-solving meadows in the sky.

##### Description

New York City handles nearly 3 million tons of trash a year. And much of it ends up on the curb in loose plastic bags — before getting shipped to landfills outside of the city altogether, on barges and then trains. This system costs the city around $500 million a year. So, can the largest city in the United States modernize its waste management?

WSJ explores how experts and city officials plan to tackle New York City’s giant trash problem.

0:34 Possible solutions

1:10 Why the issue exists

1:59 What the sanitation department does now

3:34 The bigger problem

6:13 The bigger solution

Pro Perfected

Experts in engineering and design break down a ubiquitous problem, examining how the world is built and what can make it better.

#NYC #Trash #WSJ

##### Transcript

###### NYC’s trash problem


**0:00** · Every year, New York City handles nearly three million tons of trash. For decades, mountains of garbage bags have lined the streets, feeding rats and blocking sidewalks.

**0:10** · Most people think that garbage goes up to solid waste heaven. It does quite the opposite.

**0:15** · Now, the Sanitation Department says it has a solution. Its trash revolution program aims to finally put a lid on the countless garbage bags piling city blocks.

**0:24** · But can redesigning the way New Yorkers throw out their trash solve a problem decades in the making?

**0:29** · We asked people who know the system best. Steven Cohen is the Director of the Sustainability Management Program at Columbia University, and he says one of New York's biggest solutions is surprisingly simple, changing how the city stores and collects its garbage. Instead of leaving flimsy trash bags on the sidewalk, the city's sanitation department is now moving towards sealed containers emptied by mechanized trucks.

###### Possible solutions


**0:55** · The motto of the Sanitation Department is New York's strongest. And now I think we're going to call them New York's smartest because they figured out a way to get the machine to do the work.

**1:04** · But changing how New York handles its garbage means undoing a system that's been in place for more than half a century.

###### Why the issue exists


**1:10** · We used to have metal cans that everybody had to put their garbage in that you would have to wash out after use. People in apartment buildings, superintendents didn't like doing that so much.

**1:21** · That's how New Yorkers put out their trash until the late 1960s. But when sanitation workers went on strike in 1968, residents switched to plastic garbage bags. And when the strike ended, the bags stayed.

**1:33** · This was really great news for the rats because it essentially created a buffet for them all over New York City of free food, because rats have no trouble at all getting into garbage bags.

**1:43** · More than 50 years later, trash bags are just as common as the vermin they attract, and the city's layout makes the problem even harder. Unlike other major American cities, Manhattan was built largely without alleys, leaving garbage with only one place to wait for pickup, the curb. The city is now trying to take those bags off the sidewalk altogether, replacing them with permanent containers like these.

###### What the sanitation department does now


**2:05** · The model that's used everywhere in the United States, either dumpsters in alleys, or 96 gallon sort of wheeled containers, wasn't feasible in New York City, because of our density and because of the way that our city's been built. So we looked to the model used in Europe, the stationary on-street containers, as the solution for a large number of our buildings.

**2:27** · Buildings can store trash in these bins throughout the week, and they all get emptied on pickup days.

**2:32** · You have a bin that's made of plastic, that's very durable, and there's a lot of garbage in that bin. And you have a mechanical arm picking up a tremendous amount of garbage and dumping it into the truck. The worker you see here is operating a machine and he doesn't have to go out and pick up the garbage himself.

**2:52** · And these bins seem to be working to keep out pests.

**2:55** · The pace is a little bit slower, but I think overall, I think for the community it's great. It does, we've seen the difference. I know they've been trying to tackle the rat situation, and it's definitely improved.

**3:06** · Businesses have been required to use closed bins since March 2024. And next year, the city plans to expand these residential containers to six more districts. By 2031, officials say New York City will be fully containerized.

**3:19** · This is a way to collect the garbage in a more efficient and frankly humane way, protecting the occupational health and safety of the workers. And I think this is really how robotics are changing all sorts of manual labor.

###### The bigger problem


**3:34** · In Cohen's vision for waste in the city, robotics would also play a larger role, sorting through the trash for recyclables to divert waste from landfills.

**3:42** · Humans do not want to spend their day sorting garbage. Robots could care less. And what AI can do is train those robots to really be able to identify what's coming past them. And as we get better at that, that waste stream suddenly becomes a trove of resources.

**4:02** · That could address a much larger challenge for New York. The city has nowhere to put most of its garbage.

**4:08** · The first place the waste goes in New York City is to a waste transfer station.

**4:12** · New York once relied on its own landfills, but as they filled up, the city gradually closed them. Fresh Kills, which was the largest landfill in the world at the time, closed in 2001.

**4:22** · We just ran out of space.

**4:24** · Today, New York's trash is offloaded at transfer stations, packed into shipping containers, and sent to landfills and waste-to-energy plants across the country. That process costs around $500 million per year. Waste-to-energy plants burn garbage to generate usable energy, offering an alternative to burying trash in landfills. But either way, the city still has to send its waste away.

**4:45** · In the map here, what you see is that, once we could no longer landfill in the five boroughs, we had to go outside the city. And you can see we go already 1,000 miles or longer to find a place to bring our garbage. We go wherever we can.

**5:05** · We're constantly looking.

**5:07** · That problem is only going to get worse.

**5:10** · We are going to be forced to ship our trash further and further, to places in the south and the Midwest where there's more space, there's more landfills, there's more capacity. And that's going to become really expensive.

**5:22** · Cohen's proposal could change that equation by reducing how much waste needs to be shipped out of the city in the first place.

**5:27** · The long-term vision I would have would be to build a waste processing plant that uses artificial intelligence and robotics to separate the useful resources and create separate places for those substances to be reused.

**5:46** · This concept already exists.

**5:48** · Materials processing facilities use automated systems to sort recyclables, but Cohen's proposal is more ambitious, applying that technology to New York's entire waste stream. Some tech companies are already experimenting with robots that can sort waste autonomously, separating out materials of all categories to be repurposed. In New York, Cohen says the technology would be economically transformative, using trash as a product to be sold rather than disposed of.

###### The bigger solution

**6:13** · The question is how a city as large as New York can implement this technology in the long term. The Sanitation Department has multiple programs in place for recycling and composting, but the technology is still developing. So as New York's trash disposal gets more expensive, recovering what's inside could become increasingly valuable. But making that vision a reality requires a lot more than just rethinking the city's trash collection.

**6:36** · Anything that isn't grown, anything that isn't organic is finite. And at a certain point, digging it out of the planet becomes more expensive than digging it out of your garbage.

##### Transcript

**0:01** · If you imagine a typical American city street, and you take away the space that’s dedicated to cars, you aren’t left with very much.

**0:09** · There are some narrow walkways on the side, and some bridges in between them, but not much else.

**0:13** · Cars dominate cities.

**0:16** · Spend some time walking around most cities and you’ll find yourself pushed to narrow sidewalks, waiting for crosswalk lights.

**0:20** · You’ll find cyclists navigating really narrow strips of space.

**0:23** · Americans are used to cars the way that fish are used to water.

**0:28** · That’s so ubiquitous in the U.S. that I think for most people, it just never occurred to them that it could be otherwise.

**0:35** · But what if there were a way to change that?

**0:36** · To give space back to pedestrians and bicyclists, and to make cities more friendly to life outside of a car?

**0:43** · It turns out Barcelona might have a solution.

**0:48** · In 2014, the city was faced with serious air pollution problems.

**0:51** · Barcelona and its 35 surrounding municipalities consistently failed to meet the EU’s air quality targets.

**0:57** · Studies were showing that air pollution in the region causes 3,500 premature deaths every year.

**1:03** · Traffic in the city also causes severe noise pollution.

**1:05** · So the city developed an extensive Urban Mobility Plan with the hope of reducing traffic by 21 percent.

**1:11** · The coolest part of the plan were these things: They call them "superilles".

**1:17** · Superilles?

**1:18** · “Si, superilles.”

**1:19** · That translates to “superblocks”.

**1:21** · It’s this urban design concept intended to minimize the presence of cars in city centers.

**1:26** · The word “superblock” has been used before to describe huge city blocks without any passageways for cars.

**1:31** · But that’s not what’s happening here.

**1:33** · So here’s how Barcelona’s plan works.

**1:35** · You take nine square city blocks and close off the inside to through traffic.

**1:39** · So buses, big freight trucks — or any vehicles that are trying to get from one part of town to the next — have to drive around the perimeter.

**1:47** · Inside the superblock, the speed limit is kept to 10 kilometers per hour — that translates to just over 6 miles per hour — and curbside parking is replaced by underground parking.

**1:55** · That means you wind up with street space for markets, outdoor games, and events.

**2:00** · Within this nine square block perimeter you're gonna have kind of a pleasant streetscape where people can walk around and mingle and do things without this kind of constant fear of cars around.

**2:13** · The concept is going to be tested out in five neighborhoods, but the city has identified 120 possible intersections throughout the region where it could be implemented.

**2:22** · So how do we know what the results of this kind of plan would look like?

**2:24** · Well, northwest of Barcelona is a city called Vitoria-Gasteiz, which has implemented superblock designs since 2008.

**2:30** · In the main superblock at the city center, pedestrian space increased from 45 percent of the total surface area to 74 percent.

**2:37** · With so much less traffic, noise levels dropped from 66.5 dBA to 61 dBA.

**2:43** · Most impressive of all, there was a 42% reduction in nitrogen oxide emissions and a 38% reduction in particle pollution in the area.

**2:51** · On top of that, business is up.

**2:52** · What you consistently see when people change their streetscapes to prioritize human beings over cars is you don't see any decline in economic activity, you see the opposite.

**3:03** · You get more people walking and cycling around more slowly, stopping more often patronizing businesses more, and that … center of social activity will tend to build on itself.

**3:15** · So here’s the question: could something like this work in an American city?

**3:20** · Barcelona has some unique advantages getting started on this plan, in that a lot of it was built before cars, and a lot of it was built on a simple grid.

**3:32** · The district of Eixample — where the superblock plan is based — was designed in 1859 in this repetitive grid structure by this guy, Ildefons Cerdá.

**3:41** · He basically invented the word for (and the study of) “urbanization” when he laid out this grid plan for Barcelona that evenly distributed resources like schools and hospitals.

**3:51** · But superblock designers insist that cities don’t need a simple grid structure to implement this kind of plan.

**3:56** · It can work anywhere.

**3:58** · Now, cities in the US have have attempted some car-minimizing projects like this.

**4:01** · The problem is, they’re usually done in wealthier areas with lots of existing businesses.

**4:07** · Zoning policies often require separation of residential and commercial areas — but an ideal walkable area would be a mix of the two.

**4:14** · On top of that, zoning minimums on parking availability encourage the presence of cars and parking lots, and minimums on street width make for wide, unwalkable streets.

**4:24** · Because of that, walkable districts are basically isolated luxury items in the US.

**4:29** · What makes the Barcelona plan different is that they aren’t setting aside one fancy neighborhood or town square to make pedestrian-friendly — instead, by proposing superblocks throughout the entire city, they’ve declared car-free spaces a right for everybody, no matter what part of town they're in.

**4:44** · Maybe — this might be overly optimistic — but I think it has sunk in in the U. S. that the model whereby every city resident comes with a car — and drives a car everywhere – is just inherently limited.

**4:57** · It limits the growth of your city, it limits the health of your city and the growth of your city.

**5:01** · So one way or another we have to find ways of having a lot of people live close to one another without all of them having cars.

**5:11** · You know, being able to get around and work and play in live and have enjoyable lives without cars.

#### Why did we build high-rise public housing projects

**City Beautiful**, *10 17, 2017*

##### Video (6:48)

<iframe width="560" height="315" src=https://www.youtube.com/embed/7eGTU_uXLKk title="YouTube video player" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen></iframe>

##### Description

Watch this video ad-free on Nebula: https://nebula.tv/videos/city-beautiful-why-did-we-build-high-rise-public-housing-projects

In the spring of 2007, the Chicago Housing Authority demolished the last of the 28 buildings in the Robert Taylor Homes housing project. Robert Taylor Homes is one of several high profile housing project demolitions, from St. Louis’s Pruitt-Igoe to fellow Chicago project Cabrini Green. The demolitions serve as an admission that high-rise public housing wasn’t a good idea. The housing that replaced them are all low rise projects better integrated within existing neighborhoods. So why did anyone back then think it was a good idea? Why did housing authorities build these high rise projects in the first place?

Resources on this topic:

Hunt, D. B. (2001). What Went Wrong with Public Housing in Chicago? A History of the Robert Taylor Homes. Journal of the Illinois State Historical Society, 94(1), 96–123.

"Demolished: The End of Chicago's Public Housing" by David Eads and  Helga Salinas. https://apps.npr.org/lookatthis/posts/publichousing/

"When Public Housing Was Paradise" by Joy Connelly https://openingthewindow.com/2011/06/13/when-public-housing-was-paradise-2/

"Elizabeth Wood, 93, Innovator In Early Days of Public Housing" by Bruce Lambert http://www.nytimes.com/1993/01/17/us/elizabeth-wood-93-innovator-in-early-days-of-public-housing.html

"A Brief History of Public Housing" by Jennifer Amy Stoloff https://www.researchgate.net/profile/Jennifer_Stoloff/publication/228789405_A_brief_history_of_public_housing/links/5643a68008ae9f9c13e05df6/A-brief-history-of-public-housing.pdf

Video sources:
- Archive.org, Prelinger Archives

Photo sources:
- Wikimedia Commons
- Flickr user Samuel A. Love
- Zahiri, N., Dezhdar, O., & Foroutan, M. (2016). Rethinking of Critical Regionalism in High-Rise Buildings. Buildings, 7(1), 4. https://doi.org/10.3390/buildings7010004

Filmed in sunny Sacramento, California.
